title: Privacy controls that remain understandable and enforceable across services

concept.text: The proposed innovation would let people express and revise meaningful boundaries for personal data, understand consequential exceptions, and have those boundaries enforced across participating services. A person’s choices would connect to actual system behavior rather than ending at a settings screen. The interface would explain relevant trade-offs, support explicit decisions when needed, and provide understandable evidence of whether the boundaries were respected.

As a design synthesis, the central challenge is to connect three capabilities: understanding what a privacy choice means, managing that choice as circumstances change, and verifying that services honor it. A system might predict a preferred setting to reduce repeated decisions, but a prediction would not itself establish permission or guarantee privacy. The proposed capability therefore combines an HCI advance in understandable control with systems and security advances in enforcement and auditing.

significance.text: If achieved, this would make privacy control a continuing, verifiable relationship between people and participating services. People could carry meaningful boundaries across routine interactions, revise them when necessary, and concentrate attention on consequential exceptions. The direct advance would be usable control tied to enforceable behavior; fewer prompts and lower management effort would be intended benefits requiring field evidence.

As a conditional downstream possibility, broad adoption could reduce the need to repeatedly interpret unrelated settings and reconcile inconsistent service behavior. It could also make privacy commitments easier to assess because interface promises would have corresponding evidence about data handling. These benefits would depend on service participation, interoperable interpretation of boundaries, effective enforcement, and sustained usability. Neither broad adoption nor a reduction in the burden of existing settings is established by the supplied evidence.

The scope would remain bounded. Enforceable controls across participating services would not guarantee protection against every recipient, inference, or breach. Nor would expressing a boundary eliminate future decisions: changed purposes, new services, shared data, and conflicts with functionality or other people’s interests could require revision or an explicit choice. The revolutionary possibility is dependable, manageable privacy control within demonstrated boundaries, rather than universal protection.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is an end-to-end connection between understandable privacy intentions and verifiable enforcement across services. As an engineering synthesis, this requires translating a person’s boundaries into operational rules without silently changing their meaning. Services would need compatible ways to describe relevant data uses, recognize exceptions, and respond when a requested use falls outside an existing boundary.

A corresponding HCI challenge is helping people understand consequential trade-offs without making privacy management a continuous task. The problem formulation treats preferences as context dependent and revisable, with possible conflicts involving functionality and other people. Those premises are coherent design concerns, but the supplied review could not verify their empirical grounding from retained source material. Systems would need to distinguish routine applications of an existing choice from situations where uncertainty or changed circumstances warrant renewed attention.

As a technical synthesis, enforcement must extend beyond recording a preference or deciding whether to grant access. It must account for relevant downstream handling, changes of purpose, and service changes, while producing evidence that independent auditors can assess. Concrete barriers include making data flows observable, maintaining consistent rule interpretation across service boundaries, and detecting violations despite incomplete visibility. A successful preference predictor would address only one component of this larger problem.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies the CHI 2018 paper “Contextualizing Privacy Decisions for Better Prediction (and Protection)” by Primal Wijesekera, Joel Reardon, Irwin Reyes, Lynn Tsai, Jung-Wei Chen, Nathan Good, David Wagner, Konstantin Beznosov, and Serge Egelman, DOI 10.1145/3173574.3173842. It reports a one-week Android field study involving 37 users and an analysis of validation responses from 31 users. These are reported details from the supplied research: the source index contains no captured artifact or source text, so the review could not confirm the document’s identity from its contents or inspect its methods and results.

According to that research account, contextual predictions matched prompted privacy preferences better than the comparison, while most classifier errors were erroneous grants. The comparison, quantitative performance, and error pattern remain unverified in the supplied review because the underlying passages were unavailable. The reported error direction matters: aggregate predictive improvement can coexist with mistakes that permit access a person would have refused. Missing retained evidence leaves these claims unresolved; it does not establish that they are false.

Even if the reported findings are confirmed, agreement with prompted answers would demonstrate a narrower capability than this innovation requires. Prompted answers do not by themselves establish that all relevant interests have been captured, and prediction accuracy does not establish compliant downstream data handling. Context-aware permission prediction is therefore a possible component of the proposed system, not a demonstration of understandable and enforceable privacy boundaries across services.

The supplied materials establish no broader present-day assessment of the field. The review’s empty bounded search record provides no freshness finding as of November 1, 2026, and cannot establish either that the full capability remains unsolved across all research or that it has been achieved. The dated 2018 report should be interpreted within its reported Android study scope, without treating its age as a reason to reject it.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: conduct extended, independent field studies across multiple participating services in which people set and revise privacy boundaries, explain consequential trade-offs, recognize meaningful exceptions, and check actual data flows against their choices. Compare the system with existing controls on privacy violations, task completion, comprehension, and management burden. These are proposed evaluation dimensions, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Independent multiservice field studies compare boundary enforcement and usability

completion_criteria.text: The proposed studies should include shared data, changed purposes, service changes, uncertain preferences, and situations requiring an explicit decision. Evaluation should distinguish a correctly predicted preference from a correctly enforced boundary, and distinguish comprehension of a prompt from understanding its practical consequences. It should report erroneous grants and other violations separately from aggregate accuracy so that favorable averages do not obscure consequential failures.
completion_criteria.label: Studies distinguish preference prediction from enforcement and report violations

completion_criteria.text: Independent audits should compare interface commitments, enforcement rules, and observed data handling, including relevant downstream behavior within the claimed scope. A reproducible protocol should define study duration, service coverage, violation measurement, success thresholds, and what auditors can and cannot observe. These operational choices remain to be specified. Replication across different participants and service combinations would demonstrate breadth; finite tests would not establish literal universality or protection beyond the participating systems and audited boundaries.
completion_criteria.label: Independent audits reproducibly compare commitments with scoped data handling

related_concepts.text: Based on the supplied roster titles, HCI-06, “Delegation interfaces that keep people in meaningful control of computer work,” overlaps through the need to communicate authority, expose exceptions, and support revision of delegated decisions. HCI-09 would focus specifically on personal-data boundaries and their enforcement across services. HCI-06 should not be reduced to permission setting: its stated scope is meaningful control over delegated computer work.

HCI-10, “Lifelong personal memory augmentation with controllable evidence,” has a plausible relationship because retained personal information and control over evidence can raise questions about access, use, and revision. HCI-09 could supply privacy controls relevant to such a system, while its own scope extends across ordinary computing services. The roster does not define HCI-10 simply as sensitive records, and the supplied titles alone do not establish a detailed technical dependency. These relationships are conceptual interpretations of the roster, not findings attributed to the 2018 paper.

change_log.change: Replaced expressing boundaries “once” with expressing and revising them, and limited enforcement claims to participating services.
change_log.reason: Preserves the intended reduction in repetitive decisions while accounting for changing contexts, purposes, and service coverage.

change_log.change: Made reduced burden, broad adoption, and downstream impact explicitly conditional.
change_log.reason: These are potential consequences of the proposed capability, not demonstrated outcomes in the supplied evidence.

change_log.change: Preserved the 2018 study’s reported duration, participant counts, comparative result, and erroneous-grant pattern with explicit verification limits.
change_log.reason: The review had no retained artifact or source text to inspect; missing evidence warrants qualification rather than deletion or rejection.

change_log.change: Separated preference prediction, prompted-answer agreement, permission decisions, downstream enforcement, and auditing.
change_log.reason: These capabilities support different conclusions, and improvement in one does not establish the full innovation.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration into distinct usability, enforcement, audit, and replication requirements.
change_log.reason: Integrates the review’s operational concerns while keeping unspecified thresholds clearly proposed and avoiding claims of universality.

change_log.change: Reframed the relationships with HCI-06 and HCI-10 using their supplied roster titles.
change_log.reason: The earlier descriptions as permission setting and sensitive records were narrower than the actual titles; title-based relationships can be explained without inventing detailed definitions.

change_log.change: Preserved the absence of a freshness finding separately from the dated study account.
change_log.reason: An empty search record supports neither a present-day achievement claim nor a conclusion that the capability remains universally unsolved.

unresolved_issues: The paper’s content identity, methods, one-week duration, 37-user study, 31-user validation analysis, comparison, and erroneous-grant pattern remain unverified because no captured artifact or source text was supplied.
The empirical grounding for context dependence, changing preferences, conflicting interests, and the burden of fragmented settings remains unverified in the supplied evidence.
No supplied freshness evidence establishes the broader state of the field as of November 1, 2026.
A demonstration protocol still needs study duration, service coverage, violation definitions, measurement methods, success thresholds, and explicit audit visibility limits.
Detailed technical relationships with HCI-06 and HCI-10 remain uncertain because the roster supplies titles rather than full concept definitions.

brief.title: Privacy choices that services understand and honor
possible: You could set limits on how participating services use your personal data, carry those limits between services, and revise them as your needs change. You could understand important exceptions and see understandable evidence of whether services respected your choices.
why: People would gain continuing control over their data, with choices tied to what services actually do. Privacy promises would become easier to assess. Carrying choices between services could also reduce the work of interpreting unrelated settings.

sources.showed: This is an Android field study of predicting people's privacy preferences using the circumstances of a request.
sources.cited_for: Predicting preferred settings could help people manage privacy choices.
sources.not_established: Predicting a person's answer does not establish permission or control how services subsequently handle data.

sources.showed: They tested an assistant that recommended app permissions, meaning settings that allow access to data or resources. Participants generally accepted its recommendations.
sources.quote: We find that 78.7% of the recommendations made by the PPA were adopted by users.
sources.cited_for: Personalized recommendations can help people manage mobile app permissions.
sources.not_established: Accepting recommendations does not demonstrate understanding of their consequences or enforcement across services.

sources.showed: They tested websites' responses to Global Privacy Control, a browser signal requesting an end to data sales or sharing. Many sites failed to consistently record that choice.
sources.quote:
We find that about a third of
sites that have evidence of selling or sharing personal informa-
tion per the CCPA implement at least one of the four privacy
strings.
sources.cited_for: Automated tests can check whether websites record and pass along privacy requests.
sources.not_established: Recorded requests do not prove that every recipient actually stops the prohibited data use.

sources.who: Brian Tang, Duc Bui, and Kang G. Shin
sources.showed: They built ConsentChk to compare cookie choices with website behavior. Cookies are browser records that can support tracking. The tool detected ignored rejections and other mismatches.
sources.quote:
From these measurements, we found widespread occur-
rences of cookie consent violations across all 8 regions.
sources.cited_for: Observed website behavior can reveal failures to honor explicit privacy choices.
sources.not_established: Testing cookie behavior does not establish enforcement of broader personal-data boundaries across services.

sources.who: Simon Koch, Malte Wessels, Benjamin Altpeter, Madita Olvermann, and Martin Johns
sources.showed: They compared iPhone apps' privacy labels, which describe data collection, with data the apps transmitted. Some apps sent information their labels did not declare.
sources.quote:
At least 276 of these apps
violate their privacy label by transmitting data without
declaration, showing that the privacy labels’ correctness
was not validated during the app approval process.
sources.cited_for: Actual data transmissions can be compared with public privacy promises.
sources.not_established: Detecting inaccurate labels does not prevent violations or give people enforceable control.

shown: Liu and collaborators demonstrated personalized permission advice on people's own phones. Hausladen, Tang, Koch, and their collaborators demonstrated ways to compare privacy promises or choices with observable service behavior. These are separate parts of the proposed capability.
missing: Services need shared rules that preserve the meaning of people's choices when data moves between them.
People need understandable ways to revise boundaries and decide consequential exceptions without constant attention.
Enforcement must cover later data uses and produce evidence independent auditors can assess.
Extended studies must demonstrate that understandable choices remain effective across participating services.

milestones.label: Independent field studies compare control across services
milestones.explanation: Extended independent studies would compare violations, task completion, understanding, and effort with existing controls across services. They would test whether people can set, revise, and check boundaries while understanding trade-offs.

milestones.label: Studies separate predicted choices from enforced boundaries
milestones.explanation: Studies would test shared data, changed uses and services, uncertainty, and explicit decisions, reporting unwanted access separately. They would distinguish prediction and prompt comprehension from enforcement and practical understanding.

milestones.label: Independent audits reproducibly compare promises with data handling
milestones.explanation: Independent audits would reproducibly compare promises, rules, and later data handling under defined coverage, duration, violation measures, thresholds, and visibility limits. Replication would establish breadth within those boundaries.

uncertain: How much privacy-management effort can fall while people still understand consequential choices?
What study duration, service coverage, and violation thresholds would count as success?
How much later data handling can auditors observe well enough to judge whether boundaries held?

page.title: Interoperable privacy controls
page.definition: People can set and revise understandable rules for collecting, using and sharing their personal data. Global Privacy Control already lets a browser ask websites to stop selling or sharing that data. The broader goal is for participating services to exchange and enforce current choices. A consent receipt lets a person check what they agreed to. Records of processing and disclosure let people and independent auditors check what recipients did.

goal.need: Opting out site by site makes people repeat the same decision. App privacy labels can also mislead: at least 276 of 1,687 tested iOS apps transmitted data they had not declared. A choice that carries across services can spare people repeated prompts, provided recipients act on it. In an April 2024 California web crawl, only 1,620 of 3,566 sites with evidence of sale or sharing and a measured privacy indicator reflected the opt-out in every indicator they used. Checking whether transfers stopped requires evidence of what recipients did.

figures.caption: Websites meeting the study's privacy-indicator opt-out criterion
figures.note: Eligible websites had evidence of sale/sharing and at least one measured privacy indicator. Passing meant opt-out in every implemented indicator, not verification of subsequent data use.

statements.body: National Institute of Standards and Technology
statements.quote: privacy protection should allow for individual choices, as long as effective privacy risk mitigations are already engineered into products and services.
When an opt-out mechanism exists, it should preferably work with a global opt-out mechanism.

statements.body: International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission
statements.quote: This document specifies an interoperable, open and extensible information structure for recording PII principals' consent to PII processing.
statements.context: PII is personally identifiable information; a PII principal is the person to whom it relates.

statements.quote: privacy-aware, secure workflows that include usage/access control, transparency and compliance verification
statements.context: The grant agreement was signed on 4 November 2016. Its objective also specifies recording consent at collection and giving people a dashboard to understand and control processing.

statements.quote: a minimum and non-negotiable level of privacy protection for all individuals
statements.context: Opinion 1/98 called for enforceable data protection rules alongside the proposed Platform for Privacy Preferences and Open Profiling Standard. It placed responsibility for compliance on the controller.

completion.title: A multiservice deployment passes an independent test of understandable choices and their enforcement.
completion.criterion: An independent assessment of a deployed system establishes that people understand and can revise its supported processing choices, participating services preserve those choices, and observed processing conforms to current choices after changes and revocation, with exceptions disclosed. The assessment covers interfaces, transmitted permissions, recipient processing and evidence people can inspect. It identifies the services, data uses, participants and observation period. Success is confined to that assessed scope.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; provisional synthesis of the cited requirements, rather than an externally adopted completion test.
completion.basis: Searched NIST Privacy Framework outcomes, W3C Privacy Principles and GPC conformance, ISO/IEC TS 27560's scope, California opt-out rules, and EDPB consent and Europrivacy certification documents. No single test combining user understanding, interoperable revision and verified recipient behavior was located, nor common sample-size, duration or error thresholds. The proposed test combines these supported functions within an assessed scope.

milestones.title: An organization has procedures in place to grant, maintain and revoke processing permissions.
milestones.criterion: Establish and put into practice policies, processes and procedures for authorizing data processing, maintaining those authorizations and revoking them. Authorization may come from an organizational decision or an individual's consent.
milestones.set_by: NIST, Privacy Framework Version 1.0, Appendix A, CT.PO-P1, printed page 23. The outcome appears in a table and is voluntary, not a certification test.

milestones.title: People can understand a consent request and withdraw consent as easily as they give it.
milestones.criterion: For consent-based processing, present a distinct, intelligible, accessible request in plain language appropriate to its audience. People can identify the controller and processing purposes; withdrawal is available at any time, through the same electronic interface where applicable, as easily as consent and without detriment. Recommendation adoption and preference agreement do not establish that these conditions hold.
milestones.set_by: European Data Protection Board, Guidelines 05/2020, Version 1.1, paragraphs 67–70 and 113–115; applies to consent under the GDPR.
milestones.threshold_quote: consent can be withdrawn by the data subject as easy as giving consent and at any given time.

milestones.title: A browser communicates its enabled opt-out through Sec-GPC: 1 and a matching JavaScript value.
milestones.criterion: Cache the preference when the active document begins loading on each top-level navigation. If enabled, send exactly one Sec-GPC request header with the value 1. If disabled or unset, omit the header. Set navigator.globalPrivacyControl to the cached Boolean value in both cases. Never send Sec-GPC in an HTTP trailer.
milestones.set_by: W3C Privacy Working Group, Global Privacy Control Working Draft of 24 September 2026, sections 3.2–3.4; a draft protocol for web sale/sharing opt-outs.

milestones.title: A service exposes reviewable disclosure records and data lineage for testing its privacy controls.
milestones.criterion: Make disclosure/sharing records and data provenance and lineage reviewable under CM.AW-P4/P6; test processing controls under CT.DM-P9. ConsentChk analyzed preferences on 1,312 of 1,793 banner-bearing websites from eight regions, crawled between 4 October 2024 and 12 October 2024. Its Irish baseline reported ignored rejection for 43.12% of cookies classified as containing personal information. External browser measurements do not provide service-side lineage or reveal every downstream use.
milestones.set_by: NIST, Privacy Framework Version 1.0, Appendix A, CM.AW-P4, CM.AW-P6 and CT.DM-P9, printed pages 24–25. These voluntary outcomes appear in tables.

milestones.title: A business ends sale/sharing within 15 business days and propagates opt-outs to interim recipients.
milestones.criterion: For a valid California opt-out request, stop selling or sharing the consumer's personal information as soon as feasible and within 15 business days of receipt. Notify every third party to whom the business sold or shared that information between submission and compliance. Direct each to comply and forward the request to anyone to whom it made that information available during that interval. Give the consumer a way to confirm that the business processed the request.
milestones.set_by: California Privacy Protection Agency, CCPA Regulations effective 1 January 2026, sections 7026(f)(1)–(2) and 7026(g); applies to CCPA sale/sharing opt-outs.
milestones.threshold_quote: as soon as feasibly possible, but no later than 15 business days

milestones.title: A prototype detects a mismatch between a person's privacy preferences and a site's stated practices.
milestones.criterion: Let a person set preferences for collection and use of personal data and compare them with a site's declared practices. A match permits access without interruption. A mismatch alerts the person and offers other ways to proceed.
milestones.set_by: World Wide Web Consortium, Platform for Privacy Preferences project launch, 11 June 1997, description of the prototype's behavior.
milestones.threshold_quote: the user is notified of the difference and is offered other access options to proceed.

milestones.title: People can identify who seeks their consent and understand each purpose for which it is sought.
milestones.criterion: Present the request distinctly, accessibly and in plain language suited to the audience. Identify the controllers relying on consent, each processing purpose, the types of data and the right to withdraw. Where relevant, explain consent-based automated decision-making and the risks of transfers without an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards.
milestones.set_by: European Data Protection Board, Guidelines 05/2020, version 1.1, paragraphs 64–70.
milestones.threshold_quote: easily identify who the controller is and to understand what they are agreeing to.

milestones.title: A person can withdraw consent at any time as easily as they gave it.
milestones.criterion: Inform the person of the right to withdraw before consent is given. Make withdrawal available at any time and as easy as giving consent, without detriment. When consent is obtained through a service-specific electronic interface, allow withdrawal through that same interface.
milestones.set_by: General Data Protection Regulation, Article 7(3), as interpreted by the European Data Protection Board in Guidelines 05/2020, paragraphs 113–116.
milestones.threshold_quote: It shall be as easy to withdraw as to give consent.

milestones.title: A service can transmit data elements together with their processing permissions.
milestones.criterion: Put in place a mechanism that transmits each covered data element with the permissions governing its processing and the related data values.
milestones.set_by: NIST Privacy Framework version 1.0, Appendix A, CT.DM-P7, printed page 24.
milestones.threshold_quote: processing permissions and related data values with data elements

milestones.title: A person receives a verifiable consent receipt that identifies the underlying decision.
milestones.criterion: Provide a consent receipt whose information is accurate, traceable and verifiable. Supply the information the person needs to interpret and use it. The receipt must identify the related record and its context well enough for the person to raise an inquiry or complaint with the controller or a regulator.
milestones.set_by: ISO/IEC TS 27560:2023, clauses 6.2.3.6, 6.2.3.7 and 6.2.4, for implementations providing consent receipts.
milestones.threshold_quote: information provided in the consent receipt is accurate, traceable, and verifiable.

milestones.title: A service makes disclosure records and the origin and history of data available for review.
milestones.criterion: Maintain records of data disclosures and sharing, together with information about where the data originated and how they moved or changed. Make both available for review or transmission.
milestones.set_by: NIST Privacy Framework version 1.0, Appendix A, CM.AW-P4 and CM.AW-P6, printed page 25.

milestones.title: A service tests and assesses the technical controls it uses to manage data processing.
milestones.criterion: Test the technical measures implemented to manage data processing and assess how they perform.
milestones.set_by: NIST Privacy Framework version 1.0, Appendix A, CT.DM-P9, printed page 24.

milestones.title: Withdrawal through a data recipient revokes the tokens for the affected data-sharing arrangement.
milestones.criterion: When a consumer withdraws consent through an Australian Consumer Data Right recipient's software, the software calls the data holder's arrangement revocation endpoint with the valid identifier for that arrangement. Revocation invalidates the associated access tokens, refresh tokens, or both, as applicable.
milestones.set_by: Australian Data Standards Chair, Consumer Data Standards version 1.36.0, CDR Arrangement Revocation and Revoking consent.
milestones.threshold_quote: Consent revocation MUST also revoke associated refresh and/or access tokens.

not_found: No published end-to-end success test or common comprehension, duration and error thresholds was located in the named standards and regulatory documents.
No study among the cited results independently verifies user understanding and subsequent recipient processing together across participating services.

results.finding: ConsentChk analyzed 1,312 websites; 43.12% of cookies ignored rejection.
results.detail: The external browser measurements tested cookie behavior against recorded choices, but did not expose service-side disclosure records or data lineage, or reveal every downstream use.
results.quote:
43.12% of cookies on websites
ignored users’ cookie consent rejection.

results.finding: Among 1,687 iOS apps, 352 transmitted honey data without a consent dialogue or privacy notice in the screenshot.
results.detail: Screenshots were taken after 60 seconds in a no-touch test. The study did not establish whether people could understand requests or withdraw consent as easily as they gave it.
results.quote:
352 apps are transmitting honey data (except the
OS version4) without some form of consent dialogue or
privacy notice in their screenshot.

results.finding: Of 1,687 iOS apps tested, 276 transmitted data not listed in their privacy labels.
results.detail: The study compared observed traffic with self-declared privacy labels. It did not establish service-side disclosure records or data lineage, and could not infer how transmitted data was used.
results.quote:
Overall, 276 apps transmitted data not listed in
their privacy labels.

results.finding: In the Proximus pilot, 1 of 12 participants did not remember the purpose for which consent was given.
results.detail: The walkthrough provides evidence about recall of the processing purpose. It does not establish that participants could identify the controller or that withdrawal was available as easily as consent and without detriment.
results.quote: Only one data subject did not remember any longer for which purpose consent was given.

results.finding: Among 158 websites, 35 required two or more steps to reach consent revocation.
results.detail: The paper contrasts these sites with zero steps to accept consent. It assesses revocation interfaces but does not establish all the criterion’s requirements for the initial request, withdrawal at any time, or absence of detriment.
results.quote:
35 (22.1%) websites out of 158 allow users to access the revocation option
within the same interface , but with additional obstruction, requir-
ing them 2 or more steps to revoke consent.

results.finding: In a consent-flow experiment, 41.7% of 48 parents in the timed slide recap group passed the comprehension quiz on their first attempt.
results.detail: The quiz tested understanding of selected policy terms, with a passing threshold of five out of six answers. The study does not establish controller identification or the availability and ease of withdrawing consent.
results.quote: The slide recap condition had the highest first-attempt passing rate (41.7%), and 66.4% of retakers improved.

results.finding: SPECIAL-K checked 1,200,000 synthetic streaming events with median latency below 2.5 ms.
results.detail: The benchmark tested compliance checking against synthetic policies and events. The platform describes reviewable processing and sharing logs with provenance metadata, but the evaluation does not establish service-side data lineage or test transparency access.
results.quote:
Results show that the (median) latency is
always at the level of milliseconds (in particular, less than 2.5 ms), with a noticeable improvement when
more compliance checkers are running in parallel, providing a stable latency of 1.5 ms .

results.finding: One Proximus pilot implemented a simplified event log and experimented with an ex-post compliance checker.
results.detail: The example log records a collection event and its recipient, but the report does not establish reviewable sharing records and data lineage or complete testing under the specified controls.
results.quote:
Proximus has not specifically deployed the SPLog mechanism as described in D2.7 by WU. However, it 
used the content of D2.7 as inspiration to implement a more simple derived version.

results.finding: Advertising or analytics cookies remained after revocation on 69 of 120 websites.
results.detail: This externally tests a processing-related control, but does not provide reviewable service-side disclosure records or data lineage. Cookie classification may be imperfect.
results.quote:
Out of the 120 websites where revocation
was possible within the same interface, we find AA cookies after
revocation on 69 (57.5%) websites.

results.finding: In a 35-person CURE prototype study, participants correctly answered 86% of consent comprehension questions on average.
results.detail: The questionnaire compared participants’ answers with their recorded consent. The prototype included withdrawal tasks, but the study does not establish equal ease of withdrawal or all other criterion conditions.
results.quote: More than a half of the participants answered all the questions correctly, and on average users got 86% of the questions correct.

results.finding: Of 47 participants testing the simplified consent prototype, 46.8% recalled how to withdraw consent.
results.detail: Withdrawal instructions were omitted from the consent step. The study measured recall after a simulated consent flow; it did not establish that withdrawal was as easy as giving consent or available without detriment.

results.finding: On-chain access logs: 100% event-capture fidelity vs gateway request log across 216 patient-nights and 60 role tests; no lineage.
results.detail: Access logs are append-only and queryable by authorized parties, but the paper reports no data provenance/lineage or downstream recipient testing; comparison was to an internal gateway log.
results.quote: On-chain access logs showed 100% event-capture fidelity against the independently maintained gateway request log across both deployment scenarios: every access event recorded at the application layer had a corresponding, matching entry on the permissioned ledger

results.finding: 17 survey respondents; average positive rating 78% across all questions, reflecting satisfaction with clarity.
results.detail: The survey covers clarity, brevity, and flexibility, not withdrawal ease, controller/purpose identification, or same-interface revocation without detriment.
results.quote: Survey feedback was favorable, with an average positive rating of 78% across all questions, reflecting satisfaction with the clarity, brevity, and flexibility of the platform.

results.finding: In a field study of 72 Android users, participants adopted 78.7% of the privacy assistant's app permission recommendations.
results.quote: We find that 78.7% of the recommendations made by the PPA were adopted by users.

results.finding: In a field study of 72 Android users, participants adopted 78.7% of the privacy assistant's app permission recommendations.
results.detail: The evaluation measured how participants used the permission-management tool. It did not measure whether apps adhered to the resulting settings.
results.quote: We find that 78.7% of the recommendations made by the PPA were adopted by users.

results.finding: In April 2024, 45% of 3,566 sites with evidence of sale or sharing indicated opt-out across every implemented privacy string.
results.detail: The study counted a public GPC support declaration among the privacy strings. Its measurements did not establish what recipients did with personal information.
results.quote:
In Febru-
ary 2024, this percentage decreased to 43% (1,473/3,402)
before increasing to 45% (1,620/3,566) in April 2024.

results.finding: In the December crawl, 9% of 468 sites with California-relevant GPP sections encoded a sale opt-out after GPC.
results.detail: The GPP field conveys a user's sale opt-out status. The crawler did not trace the field alongside individual personal data values.
results.quote:
In December 2023,
after a GPC signal was sent, 9% (44/468) of sites opted the
user out of selling.

results.finding: In April 2024, 10% of 3,402 sites assessed had inconsistent GPC opt-out indications across their implemented privacy strings.
results.detail: The inconsistency analysis covered the US Privacy String, Global Privacy Platform String, and OptanonConsent cookie. It excluded the public GPC support declaration.
results.quote:
This
percentage increased to 12% (400/3,246) in February 2024
before decreasing to 10% (338/3,402) in April 2024.

results.finding: Across 40 validation sites, manual checks reproduced 92.1% of ConsentChk’s ignored-rejection cookie detections.
results.detail: The researchers selected sites where the crawler had already detected ignored rejections. The percentage measures reproduction of flagged cookies in that sample.
results.quote:
We manually reproduced and verified that
92.1% of cookies with Ignored Cookie Rejection, 91.2% with
Undeclared Cookies, and 87% with Wrong Cookie Category
were detected by ConsentChk.

results.finding: In a 1,793-site study, 47.35% of cookies classified as likely containing personal information were undeclared.
results.detail: The 1,793 sites are the overall study sample. The percentage is calculated over cookies classified as likely containing personal information.
results.quote:
We found that undeclared cookies constituted 47.35% of per-
sonal information cookies on websites.

results.finding: In a 1,793-site audit, 96.18% of websites accessed from Ireland showed at least one cookie consent violation.
results.detail: The audit measured cookie behavior under the study’s definitions. The 1,793-site sample spans all eight regions, while the reported percentage is specific to Ireland.
results.quote:
Specifically, we found that 96.18% of websites ac-
cessed in the EU contain at least one cookie consent violation.

results.finding: Among 1,687 iOS apps tested at launch, 192 displayed a consent dialogue, privacy policy, or privacy notice.
results.detail: The screen check counted privacy notices and policies alongside consent dialogues. A single screenshot could miss a request that appeared only after interaction.
results.quote:
Overall, 192 apps displayed
a message ﬁtting our criteria.

results.finding: With tracking permission withheld, 282 of 1,687 iOS apps transmitted the all-zero advertising identifier.
results.detail: Each app ran for one minute without interaction. The all-zero value shows the identifier returned under the tested setting. Other tracking mechanisms fall outside that result.
results.quote:
We searched the collected traﬃc records and found
282 apps transmitting this all-0 IDFA value

results.finding: Across five policy-evolution use cases, the consent framework modeled how processing permissions are granted, maintained and revoked.
results.detail: The overlapping-consent example also shows that retroactive withdrawal can end access to previously collected data when no other applicable consent remains.
results.quote:
the act to collect or access may be attributed to any of the overlapping 
consents that authorize the event.

results.finding: The consent verifier took 6.7 seconds to query collection and access after a simulated year for one data subject, averaged over five runs.
results.detail: The realistic scenario assumed daily checks, weekly changes to data types and recipients, and consent changes every 90 days.
results.quote:
the time to query the knowledge base for collection and access based on the realistic scenario at 
90 days is 2.7 seconds for one data subject, and after one year is 6.7 seconds.

results.finding: The CNE pilot offered 3 places to grant or withdraw consent. The internal participant count was unreported.
results.detail: The three places were during installation, before a speed test and in settings.
results.quote:
The app had three places to give/withdraw consent: during installation, before speed test 
execution and in the settings menu.

results.finding: In the Events Nearby walkthrough, 11 of 12 participants recalled the purpose for which they gave consent.
results.detail: Participants separately reported that controller and processor labels in the Privacy Dashboard were too technical.
results.quote: Only one data subject did not remember any longer for which purpose consent was given.

results.finding: The CNE pilot offered 3 in-app locations to give or withdraw consent. The internal participant count was unreported.
results.detail: The pilot also offered withdrawal through the linked Privacy Dashboard.
results.quote:
The app had three places to give/withdraw consent: during installation, before speed test 
execution and in the settings menu.

results.finding: The CNE pilot sent 3 data fields for additional use and linked the payload to its consent policy at the SPECIAL server. The transfer count was unreported.
results.detail: The report describes sticky policies at the SPECIAL server and states that an end-to-end implementation was still unavailable.
results.quote:
Thus only there three fields of the data set are transferred to the SPECIAL 
server (for analysis by Motionlogic).

results.finding: CNE pilot users could review collection and trace sharing and use in the dashboard. The internal participant count was unreported.
results.detail: The report describes a small internal pilot. Some users found the dashboard confusing or overly detailed.
results.quote:
Being able to review the data col lection 
and even trace the share and use of one’s data was most interesting for our users

results.finding: All 4 compliance-checking techniques tested in Refinitiv's Know-Your-Customer pilot worked.
results.detail: The report gives qualitative performance comparisons. Some legal judgments still required attestations from the Privacy Office.
results.quote:
All worked. The first opti on, as exemplified by TenForce's compliance engine, has the performance 
profile that makes it the preferred option to check consent compliance in real-time.

results.finding: Of 136 TCF websites supporting withdrawal, 17 still returned positive consent through the API afterward.
results.detail: The result concerns the permission exposed by the API. Other stores and network messages could carry different values.
results.quote:
In the websites with the TCF, 17 (12.5%) out of 136
websites provide positive consent in the __tcfapi,

results.finding: Of 158 reachable Tranco websites, 35 required extra steps to reach withdrawal within the same interface.
results.detail: The step count measures how users reach the withdrawal option. The headline uses the counts in Section 5.1.2 and Table 4. Table 1 gives a different count.
results.quote:
35 (22.1%)
websites out of 158 allow users to access the revocation option
within the same interface , but with additional obstruction, requir-
ing them 2 or more steps to revoke consent.

results.finding: Advertising or analytics cookies were present after withdrawal on 69 of 120 websites offering same-interface withdrawal.
results.detail: The researchers classified cookies with CookieBlock and identified a possible source of classification error. The result concerns browser cookies observed after withdrawal.
results.quote:
Out of the 120 websites where revocation
was possible within the same interface, we find AA cookies after
revocation on 69 (57.5%) websites.

results.finding: KidsZone timed slide recap (n=48): 41.7% of parents met the first-attempt comprehension threshold.
results.detail: The recap combined repeated exposure, simplified explanations, illustrations, and pacing. Its first-attempt pass rate did not reliably exceed the plain-text control after correction for multiple comparisons.
results.quote: The slide recap condition had the highest first-attempt passing rate (41.7%), and 66.4% of retakers improved.

results.finding: SPECIAL-K’s third release supported listing and exporting disclosure records in one platform implementation.
results.detail: The provenance vocabulary describes log metadata. The BeFit example illustrates how data lineage could be reviewed, but the report gives no measured sample for the listing or export functions.

results.finding: SPECIAL-K’s compliance checker reached 3,489 events/s on a batch of 10 million synthetic events.
results.detail: The evaluation measured a compliance checker on synthetic workloads. At the highest streaming rate, events queued and maximum latency reached 17 minutes.
results.quote: maximum of 3,489 events/s in the case of 10M events.

results.finding: Sieve implemented access grants, updates and revocation in a proof of concept with two web services.
results.detail: After a service decrypts data, it can retain or share its own copy even after Sieve revokes access to the stored copy.
results.quote:
As a proof of concept, we integrated
Sieve with two open-source web services, demonstrating
that Sieve is a practical approach for restricting access to
sensitive user data.

results.finding: Sieve's Piwigo test uploaded one photo with three tags used for attribute-based access.
results.detail: Object tags describe the data. The separately issued key encodes the service's access policy.
results.quote:
To test the end-to-end performance, we uploaded a
375 KB photo which had three tags (location, date, and
username).

results.finding: Sieve access queries over one million metadata blocks averaged 0.13 ms.
results.detail: Each query used five random attributes combined with ANDs and ORs. Tests ran on one machine with servers on the loopback interface.
results.quote:
Each query
took 0.13 ms to complete on average.

results.finding: Across 35 CURE participants, the average score on questions about what processing they had agreed to was 86%.
results.detail: The questionnaire checked answers against each participant’s recorded choices. It did not directly test whether participants could identify every controller relying on consent.
results.quote:
More than a half of the participants answered
all the questions correctly, and on average users got 86% of the questions correct.

results.finding: In a 35-person CURE study, scripted tasks that included withdrawing consent averaged 1 second each.
results.detail: The average pools grant, withdrawal and overview tasks. It does not isolate withdrawal time or compare it directly with grant time.
results.quote:
The participants required, on
average, 1 second to complete each of the tasks.

results.finding: Among 16 moderated interview participants shown a CDR receipt, just under half expected a confirmation or record of the sharing arrangement.
results.detail: The study used a fictional data recipient. Some participants wanted more specific account information, recipient contact details or accreditation information.
results.quote: The majority of round 2-3 moderated interview participants valued receiving the CDR receipt, with just under half stating that they expected to receive a confirmation or record of the sharing arrangement.

results.finding: In the simplified banking-data consent prototype, 83.0% of 47 participants correctly recalled the purpose.
results.detail: The purpose result covers a simulated personal finance service. Recollection was measured directly after the prototype task.

results.finding: In the simplified CDR consent prototype, 46.8% of 47 participants correctly recalled how to withdraw.
results.detail: The report identified withdrawal methods as one of two criteria contributing to the statistically significant decrease in subjective comprehension.

results.finding: LexisNexis Risk Solutions reported a median response time of 1 day for 34,102 CCPA sale or sharing opt-out requests in 2025.
results.detail: The report gives aggregate response times. It provides no per-request cessation times and does not specify whether the reported days are business days.
results.quote: Median Number of Days to Respond to Requests to Opt-Out: 1

results.finding: IoT2Wallets made correct authorization decisions in all 200 consent-verification transactions.
results.detail: The result covers clinician access through the pilot gateway. Administrative access was governed by host defaults.
results.quote: All 200 consent-verification transactions returned the correct result across both deployment scenarios.

results.finding: In 200 IoT2Wallets verification and revocation tests, gateway revocation took at most one block confirmation in each revocation case.
results.detail: The paper gives a combined test count and does not isolate the number of revocation cases.
results.quote: Consent revocation propagated to the gateway within one block confirmation time in every test case, and no FHIR resource was released after revocation

results.finding: IoT2Wallets access logs matched 100% of gateway access events across 216 patient-nights and 60 role-based cases.
results.detail: Fidelity was measured against the gateway request log. That comparison covers gateway-recorded access and leaves downstream disclosures and data lineage unverified.
results.quote: On-chain access logs showed 100% event-capture fidelity against the independently maintained gateway request log across both deployment scenarios

results.finding: IoT2Wallets credential verification averaged 95 ms across 200 test transactions.
results.detail: The measurements apply to the institutional testbed. The study did not perform concurrency or load testing or an independent smart-contract audit.
results.quote: Table 3  reports latency across 200 test transactions per operation. All figures below were measured on the four-node Besu testbed described in  Section 2.9 , using data volumes and access patterns drawn from the clinical pilot; they are testbed measurements, not production latencies from a live hospital deployment.

results.finding: Of 44 ATHENA platform users, 25 authorized release of their contact details to the COVID OZ-Genetics study team.
results.detail: The 25 refers to users who authorized contact-detail release. The abstract's count of trial registrations describes a different outcome.
results.quote: A total of 44 (75%) logged onto the platform (indicating use), and 25 (57%) of these expressed interest in the new research study and gave consent for their contact details to be released to the OZ-Genetics study team.

results.finding: In the 44-user ATHENA pilot, 25 authorized release of contact details through a workflow that provided a digital consent receipt.
results.detail: The 25 counts consent decisions. The paper gives no separate count of receipts delivered, opened or verified.
results.quote: Consent is submitted via a digital signature ( Figure 3 ), and participants are provided a digital receipt, which can be viewed within the dynamic consent platform.

results.finding: Of 17 ATHENA survey respondents, 82% agreed that the information presented during the consent process was clear.
results.detail: The survey measured perceived clarity. It did not test whether respondents could correctly identify the controller or explain the purpose.

results.finding: The 44-user ATHENA pilot offered withdrawal in the same web platform used to give consent.
results.detail: The paper describes the implemented feature and gives no withdrawal test or comparison of the effort required for the two actions.
results.quote: In our platform, this was realized through a flexible consent model that enables digital consent, withdrawal, and revision of consent in response to new data requests.

results.finding: The ATHENA platform piloted with 44 users made data changes viewable in audit logs.
results.detail: The study gives no audit-log sample size or example tracing an actual disclosure.
results.quote: All data were stored in Queensland Health, and all data changes were audited and can be viewed via comprehensive audit logs.

results.finding: In ATHENA's live test, 25 of 44 platform users used the consent workflow to authorize release of their contact details.
results.detail: The measured outcome was submission of authorization. The study gives no test result for whether the subsequent release followed the recorded choice.
results.quote: A total of 44 (75%) logged onto the platform (indicating use), and 25 (57%) of these expressed interest in the new research study and gave consent for their contact details to be released to the OZ-Genetics study team.

results.finding: Privacy Bird flagged 50% of 588 P3P-enabled websites as mismatches at the medium privacy setting.
results.detail: The July 2005 draft was under review. The 50% measures how often the medium setting flagged a site, rather than the accuracy of mismatch detection.
results.quote:
This study found that 25% of sites received red 
birds on the low setting, 50% of sites received red birds on the medium setting, and 82% 
of sites received red birds on the high setting [9].

results.finding: The website-form prototype generated a 1-kilobyte signed consent receipt and stored the user's copy in a browser extension. Sample size unreported.
results.detail: The evaluation focused on receipt generation and performance. It did not establish whether a recipient could interpret the receipt and use it to identify the controller's record in an inquiry or complaint.
results.quote:
After this step, the actual receipts are generated,
and for the user, stored locally by the browser extension (as
shown in Figure 3).

results.finding: The ADDN Consent prototype offers 1-click subproject withdrawal in the same mobile app used to opt in. No participants were tested.
results.detail: The authors describe withdrawal as available at any time, but their mock subproject workflow only explicitly permits changes before the data-load cutoff.
results.quote: Patients can withdraw their consent at any time by simply clicking a button, and the withdrawal action is as easy as the consent action.

results.finding: In a 20-person website usability study, withdrawing cookie consent took 21 times as long as giving it, on average.
results.detail: Participants who gave consent were asked to withdraw it on one to three sites, depending on session time. The study used convenience sampling.
results.quote: On average, it took 21 times longer to withdraw consent than to give it.

results.finding: Firefox 144 showed no true navigator.globalPrivacyControl value without the Sec-GPC header across 8 preference combinations.
results.detail: The source separately reports a mismatch in Camoufox on Windows. Its fingerprint configuration produced a false page value, a true worker value, and no Sec-GPC header.
results.quote: Measured on Firefox 144: default is false, false and no header; with GPC enabled it is true, true and Sec-GPC: 1; a sweep of all eight combinations of Firefox's GPC and Do-Not-Track preferences could not produce a true property without the header.

results.finding: On one site across three Brave policy configurations, enabled GPC sent Sec-GPC: 1 and returned true in JavaScript.
results.detail: The unconfigured enterprise policy left GPC enabled by default, so that case did not test an unset browser preference.
results.quote:
confirmed
Sec-GPC: 1
header is sent with network requests
confirmed that
navigator.globalPrivacyControl
javascript call on a page returns true

results.finding: One Excel prototype demonstrated remote transfer of labeled spreadsheet values with their governing processing permissions.
results.detail: The paper demonstrates a proof of concept in a spreadsheet-sharing workflow using a TPM simulator. It gives no sample size for successful transfers. The source is an IEEE conference proceedings paper, represented as report because the schema has no conference category.
results.quote:
Data transfer is represented by the encrypted policy-data
package and accompanying key in Figure 1. The system is
capable of transferring subsets of data to match the security
on the receiving end of the transfer.

results.finding: DETECTIVE reconstructed and displayed 3 disclosures in an audit of 1 X-ray image.
results.detail: The simulated audit exposed a stale watermark. Broader testing of watermark robustness and extractability was left for future work. The supplied text identifies the paper as conference proceedings and gives no peer-review status.
results.quote:
The results of auditing an image found in the
pharmaceutical company reveal that data consumer and
provider commitments and identities are the same in the
last two disclosures (disclosure 3 and disclosure 2),
which prove that the foreign clinic had violated the
protocol.

results.finding: Companies sent processing confirmations for 121 of 210 California opt-out requests submitted by Consumer Reports as an authorized agent.
results.detail: The 7-business-day average measures response time. The pilot did not verify when sale or sharing stopped or track notices and forwarding to downstream recipients.
results.quote: In 121 cases, the company sent a confirmation that the opt out had been processed.

results.finding: MaxMind’s 173,682 CCPA sale or sharing opt-out requests in 2025 had a median closure time of 4.0 days.
results.detail: The table reports aggregate closure times in unspecified days and groups full and partial compliance together. It provides neither the time to cessation nor the number of requests that exceeded 15 business days.

results.finding: Redbark reports real-time bank data access revocation after withdrawal through Fiskil’s dashboard. Sample size and measured latency are unspecified.
results.detail: The page describes production behavior. Queued token deletion does not establish that the data holder invalidated the arrangement’s tokens.
results.quote: Withdrawal is real-time: it revokes data access at the bank, disables every sync that depends on that consent, and queues deletion of the associated connection data, tokens, and any data derived from it, such as rule suggestions.

definition = "People can set and revise understandable rules for collecting, using and sharing their personal data. Global Privacy Control already lets a browser ask websites to stop selling or sharing that data. The broader goal is for participating services to exchange and enforce current choices. A consent receipt lets a person check what they agreed to. Records of processing and disclosure let people and independent auditors check what recipients did.". Reason: The definition gains a deployed example and explains what a consent receipt lets a person check.

goal.need = "Opting out site by site makes people repeat the same decision. App privacy labels can also mislead: at least 276 of 1,687 tested iOS apps transmitted data they had not declared. A choice that carries across services can spare people repeated prompts, provided recipients act on it. In an April 2024 California web crawl, only 1,620 of 3,566 sites with evidence of sale or sharing and a measured privacy indicator reflected the opt-out in every indicator they used. Checking whether transfers stopped requires evidence of what recipients did.". Reason: The current paragraph reports two measurements but omits the benefit of carrying one choice across services and the condition for that choice to protect anyone.

add statement by European Union Horizon 2020, SPECIAL project, 2016: "privacy-aware, secure workflows that include usage/access control, transparency and compliance verification". Reason: The SPECIAL grant objective connects user choices to verification of subsequent processing, which the existing statements address separately.

add statement by Article 29 Data Protection Working Party, 1998: "a minimum and non-negotiable level of privacy protection for all individuals". Reason: The Working Party identifies a limit on what negotiated privacy preferences can achieve without enforceable baseline protections.

add milestone after None: "A prototype detects a mismatch between a person's privacy preferences and a site's stated practices.". Reason: The earliest milestone currently misses the prototype-level ability to compare a person's rules with a service's declared practices.

edit m1: title = "An organization has procedures in place to grant, maintain and revoke processing permissions."; criterion = "Establish and put into practice policies, processes and procedures for authorizing data processing, maintaining those authorizations and revoking them. Authorization may come from an organizational decision or an individual's consent."; threshold_quote = "revoking authorizations, and maintaining authorizations"; threshold_ref = 3; refs = [3]. Reason: The current criterion embeds two device-permission studies and describes software functionality where NIST specifies organizational policies, processes and procedures.

split m2 into "People can identify who seeks their consent and understand each purpose for which it is sought." | "A person can withdraw consent at any time as easily as they gave it.". Reason: Understanding a request before agreeing and withdrawing consent afterward are distinct results with separate requirements and evidence.

edit m3: criterion = "Cache the preference when the active document begins loading on each top-level navigation. If enabled, send exactly one Sec-GPC request header with the value 1. If disabled or unset, omit the header. Set navigator.globalPrivacyControl to the cached Boolean value in both cases. Never send Sec-GPC in an HTTP trailer."; threshold_quote = "exactly the numeric character \"1\""; threshold_ref = 7; refs = [7]. Reason: The browser test omits the draft's trailer prohibition and includes a website crawl that measured a different result.

add milestone after m3: "A service can transmit data elements together with their processing permissions.". Reason: The browser signal covers one general preference, while NIST separately identifies transmission of permissions with the particular data they govern.

add milestone after m1: "A person receives a verifiable consent receipt that identifies the underlying decision.". Reason: The definition promises evidence people can inspect, but no milestone tests whether a person can use a receipt to identify and question their consent record.

split m4 into "A service makes disclosure records and the origin and history of data available for review." | "A service tests and assesses the technical controls it uses to manage data processing.". Reason: Maintaining reviewable records and testing a technical control are independently assessable NIST outcomes, and the cookie-crawl figures define neither.

edit m5: criterion = "For a valid California opt-out request, stop selling or sharing the consumer's personal information as soon as feasible and within 15 business days of receipt. Notify every third party to whom the business sold or shared that information between submission and compliance. Direct each to comply and forward the request to anyone to whom it made that information available during that interval. Give the consumer a way to confirm that the business processed the request."; refs = [8]. Reason: California's notice duty covers third parties to whom information was sold or shared in the interim, and the observation about browser measurements is evidence commentary.

add milestone after m5: "Withdrawal through a data recipient revokes the tokens for the affected data-sharing arrangement.". Reason: Australia's Consumer Data Standards supply a cross-service withdrawal test with an observable consequence for continued access.
